headings.title: Introduction and Phases of Search and Rescue Operations
headings.content: Search and Rescue forms a critical component of disaster response, aiming to locate lost or trapped individuals and deliver them to safety. Operations follow a structured sequence starting with the **search** phase, which uses reconnaissance and canine units to find victims, moving into the **rescue** phase focused on extrication, and concluding with medical stabilization. Success depends heavily on speed, specialized training, and multidisciplinary coordination among emergency services.

headings.title: Roles of Nursing and Medical Personnel
headings.content: Nurses operating within a search and rescue framework extend critical care skills directly into pre-hospital and disaster zones. Their responsibilities include establishing casualty collection points, administering life-saving interventions under austere conditions, and coordinating patient tracking. Unlike standard hospital duties, disaster nursing requires rapid improvisations, adherence to strict personal protective measures, and seamless collaboration with firefighters and paramedics.

headings.title: Triage and Initial Assessment Protocols
headings.content:
Mass casualty incidents require rapid sorting of victims using systematic triage frameworks. The **START** (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) protocol uses respiratory rate, perfusion, and mental status to categorize patients within seconds.

- **Red (Immediate)**: Life-threatening injuries requiring urgent intervention.
- **Yellow (Delayed)**: Serious injuries needing care, but stable for a short period.
- **Green (Minor)**: Walking wounded who can wait for treatment.
- **Black (Expectant/Deceased)**: Fatal injuries where survival is unlikely given available resources.

headings.title: Equipment, Gear, and Rescuer Safety
headings.content: Rescuer safety remains the absolute priority during any operation; an injured rescuer compounds the emergency. Personal protective equipment must include reinforced helmets, steel-toed boots, high-visibility vests, and respiratory masks depending on environmental hazards. Communication devices, portable lighting, and lightweight trauma kits must be routinely inspected before deployment into collapsed structures or disaster zones.

headings.title: Pre-Hospital Stabilization and Emergency Care
headings.content: Stabilizing patients in the field focuses on addressing immediate threats to life following the ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure). Nurses and medics manage severe hemorrhage using tourniquets, clear obstructed airways, and apply cervical collars when spinal injury is suspected. Because definitive surgical care may be hours away, continuous monitoring and aggressive prevention of hypothermia are essential.

headings.title: Evacuation and Patient Transport Strategies
headings.content: Moving stabilized patients out of hazardous zones requires appropriate transport modalities and secure immobilization. Depending on terrain and accessibility, teams use stretchers, backboards, all-terrain vehicles, or air ambulances. Nurses must secure intravenous lines, secure oxygen tanks, and ensure continuous vital sign monitoring throughout the bumpy journey to a definitive care facility.

headings.title: Psychological Support and Debriefing
headings.content: Disaster response exposes rescue personnel and survivors to extreme psychological trauma, grief, and high-stress environments. Psychological first aid should be offered immediately to survivors to restore calm and meet basic human needs. Post-operation debriefings for nursing and medical staff help process traumatic events, mitigate burnout, and screen for early signs of post-traumatic stress disorder.
